stem: A platform team's service runs Claude Code non-interactively with claude -p for each incoming job. Claude Code tracing is enabled and exports to the same OpenTelemetry backend as the service. In the backend, every Claude Code interaction appears as its own root trace, so engineers cannot follow a slow job from the service's request span into the model calls and tool executions it caused. Which change links them?

options.text: Pass the service's active W3C trace context into the subprocess environment as TRACEPARENT, which non-interactive sessions read as their parent.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_PROPAGATE_TRACEPARENT so Claude Code forwards trace context on its outbound model requests through the service's proxy.
Enable OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS so spans carry tool inputs and commands, letting engineers correlate each job's spans by matching their content.
Lower the span export interval so Claude Code flushes its spans before the service closes its request span and the backend finalizes it.

explanation: In Agent SDK and non-interactive -p sessions, Claude Code reads TRACEPARENT and TRACESTATE from its own environment when starting each interaction span, so an embedding process can pass its active W3C trace context and Claude Code's spans appear as children of the caller's trace. Interactive sessions deliberately ignore inbound TRACEPARENT.

distractorNotes.b: That switch governs the traceparent header Claude Code sends outbound through a custom base URL; it links Claude Code to downstream services, not to its caller.
distractorNotes.c: Tool detail logging changes what content spans carry, not how traces are parented, and matching on content is not trace propagation.
distractorNotes.d: Export timing affects when spans arrive, not their parent; spans without inbound context stay root spans however quickly they are flushed.

sourceNote: Traces (beta): -p and Agent SDK sessions read TRACEPARENT/TRACESTATE from the environment to join the caller's trace

stem: A platform team deploys Claude Code across an enterprise engineering organization using a managed settings file that sets OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT to route telemetry to a central collector. An engineer attempts to redirect event streams by configuring OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT in their personal ~/.claude/settings.json file to point to a local logging proxy. What happens when the engineer starts Claude Code?

options.text: Claude Code prioritizes the user-level settings file for log signals and routes log events to the local proxy while sending metrics to the managed endpoint.
Claude Code removes the user-configured per-signal endpoint variable at startup and exports both metrics and logs exclusively to the collector defined in managed settings.
Claude Code detects the conflicting collector endpoint definitions during initialization and terminates with a configuration validation error until the local settings file is amended.
Claude Code merges the endpoints by sending a duplicate stream of all event log records to the local proxy while maintaining the primary managed export.

explanation: When an administrator configures OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT in managed settings, Claude Code automatically removes developer-set per-signal endpoint variables (such as OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_LOGS_ENDPOINT or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_METRICS_ENDPOINT) at startup and logs a warning in the debug log. This mechanism prevents individual developers from redirecting specific telemetry signals away from the organization's designated OpenTelemetry collector.

distractorNotes.a: Settings precedence does not allow user settings to override collector endpoints when managed settings lock the generic OTLP destination; Claude Code explicitly strips conflicting signal endpoints.
distractorNotes.c: Conflicting developer endpoints do not prevent process startup or cause fatal validation errors; Claude Code strips the developer's setting and continues running with the managed endpoint.
distractorNotes.d: Claude Code exports each signal to a single configured destination rather than splitting or duplicating streams across conflicting endpoints.

sourceNote: Managed settings OTLP endpoint locking: removes developer-set per-signal endpoints at startup

stem: A developer building a customer support agent with the Claude Agent SDK in TypeScript wants to inspect telemetry events in real time. In the agent configuration, they set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY to 1 and set OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER to console. When executing queries against the agent, the application fails to receive assistant message chunks and throws JSON stream parsing exceptions. Why does this exporter selection break the SDK?

options.text: The console exporter requires dedicated synchronous file descriptors that block the Node.js asynchronous event loop during active streaming model generation.
The Agent SDK requires OTLP protobuf formatting and rejects text-based telemetry formatting across all exporter channels.
The console exporter writes telemetry output directly to standard output, which the Agent SDK uses as its inter-process communication channel.
The underlying Claude Code CLI process disables the console exporter whenever child process mode is invoked by an external wrapper.

explanation: The Claude Agent SDK runs the Claude Code CLI as a child process and communicates with it over standard input and standard output. The console exporter writes telemetry data directly to standard output, which injects unstructured telemetry logs into the SDK's structured message protocol stream, corrupting the message channel and causing parse failures.

distractorNotes.a: The failure is not related to event loop blocking or synchronous file descriptors; rather, telemetry logs sent to standard output corrupt the IPC protocol stream.
distractorNotes.b: The SDK does not mandate OTLP protobuf over other formats for internal parsing; the issue is that standard output is reserved for IPC messages rather than console logs.
distractorNotes.d: The CLI does not automatically disable the console exporter when run as a child process; it executes the configured exporter, which pollutes the communication stream.

sourceNote: Agent SDK telemetry: do not use console exporter because stdout is used as the SDK message channel

stem: An enterprise healthcare organization configures OpenTelemetry export in the Claude Console to send API traces to their central observability vendor. The organization has an active HIPAA data-handling agreement with Anthropic. Administrators configure an OpenTelemetry destination with the content mode explicitly set to Full content. Which TWO statements accurately describe how trace payloads and content limits are handled for this organization?

options.text: The API destination exports metadata only, overriding the Full content setting due to the active HIPAA data-handling agreement.
Spans that exceed payload limits prioritize retaining system instructions and earliest conversation turns while truncating recent tool outputs.
SDK client spans sent from customer infrastructure are automatically blocked from exporting prompt content by the central API destination policy.
Under standard Full content mode without data restrictions, request spans that exceed the default 0.75 MB limit drop system prompts and earliest messages first.
The API destination buffers uncompressed conversation payloads up to 4 MB per trace before applying lossy compaction to tool result blocks.

explanation: For organizations with HIPAA, FERPA, or K-12 data-handling restrictions with Anthropic, API trace destinations export only metadata regardless of the configured content mode (though client-side SDK spans emitted from customer infrastructure remain unaffected). In standard environments where Full content is active, each span holds up to 0.75 MB by default; when content exceeds this threshold, request spans drop the system prompt and earliest messages first, tool spans drop blocks from the end of results, and anthropic.content.truncated is set to true.

distractorNotes.b: When request content exceeds payload limits, the SDK and API drop the system prompt and earliest messages first, rather than preserving them at the expense of recent outputs.
distractorNotes.c: Regulatory restrictions on API destinations do not affect SDK client spans emitted from self-hosted customer code; those are governed by the local SDK client configuration.
distractorNotes.e: The default per-span payload limit is 0.75 MB rather than 4 MB; 4 MB is the approximate size needed for an entire 1M-token context window if limits are manually expanded.

sourceNote: OTel content modes: HIPAA restriction forces metadata only; Full content truncates request spans earliest messages first at 0.75 MB

stem: An analytics engineering team ingests Claude Code metrics and spans into a central observability lakehouse formatted around OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions. When comparing token metrics, engineers observe that input token counts exported by Claude Code are substantially lower than billing records for identical sessions. How must the team calculate gen_ai.usage.input_tokens from Claude Code telemetry to align with the semantic conventions?

options.text: Multiply input_tokens by the active model compression factor derived from the prompt caching header ratio.
Sum input_tokens, cache_read_tokens, and cache_creation_tokens from the span or event attributes.
Extract input_tokens directly because Claude Code pre-aggregates cache hits into the primary usage counter.
Subtract cache_read_tokens from input_tokens to isolate uncached contextual prompt overhead.

explanation: Claude Code exports input token counts directly as returned in the API usage block, where input_tokens excludes tokens read from or written to the prompt cache. The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions specify that gen_ai.usage.input_tokens must include all input tokens (uncached, cache reads, and cache writes). To match the convention, backends must sum input_tokens, cache_read_tokens, and cache_creation_tokens.

distractorNotes.a: There is no model compression multiplier in OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions; token counts are exact sums of uncached and cached token attributes.
distractorNotes.c: Claude Code does not pre-aggregate cached tokens into input_tokens; its input_tokens attribute explicitly excludes cache read and creation tokens.
distractorNotes.d: Subtracting cache reads further reduces the count rather than reconstructing the total prompt token volume required by the GenAI semantic conventions.

sourceNote: GenAI semantic conventions mapping: sum input_tokens, cache_read_tokens, and cache_creation_tokens

stem: A site reliability engineering team monitors an automated triage service powered by Claude Code. The team configures alerts on HTTP error codes and claude_code.api_error log events. During a security audit, several sensitive prompts are declined by the model, but no alerts trigger and the HTTP status remains 200. How should the team configure alerting to capture model refusals?

options.text: Configure monitoring for HTTP 403 Forbidden status codes on the inbound API gateway reverse proxy.
Set an alert on claude_code.api_retries_exhausted with the error classification category filtered specifically to safety policy violations.
Monitor for claude_code.api_refusal events emitted when the response stream terminates with a refusal stop reason.
Inspect claude_code.tool.execution spans for error status codes generated during safety classifier evaluation.

explanation: Model refusals arrive on a successful HTTP 200 response stream with stop_reason set to 'refusal' rather than as an HTTP error status code. Consequently, api_error events do not fire. Claude Code emits a dedicated claude_code.api_refusal event for these occurrences, allowing observability systems to track refusal rates and categories independently of operational API failures.

distractorNotes.a: Model refusals return successful HTTP 200 responses with a refusal stop reason; they do not generate HTTP 403 Forbidden status codes at the gateway.
distractorNotes.b: The api_retries_exhausted event fires only when an API call fails repeatedly on operational errors; it is not emitted for model refusals.
distractorNotes.d: Refusals are generated during model inference rather than tool execution, so tool execution spans do not capture refusal stop reasons.

sourceNote: API refusal events: refusals return HTTP 200, emitting claude_code.api_refusal rather than api_error

stem: A platform team enables both Anthropic SDK tracing and Claude API tracing to achieve full client and server visibility into their Messages API calls. An automated pipeline aggregates token usage from all emitted OpenTelemetry spans. The resulting dashboard shows daily token consumption at approximately double the volume reported on the official Claude Console invoice. What is the root cause of this discrepancy?

options.text: The pipeline sums token attributes across both CLIENT and SERVER spans named anthropic.messages.create, double-counting every request.
The API server span reports uncompressed prompt tokens while the SDK client span reports compressed tokens after semantic deduplication.
Prompt caching attributes are calculated using different multipliers on client spans compared to server spans in the OpenTelemetry exporter.
The Anthropic SDK automatically duplicates token counters on client spans whenever request retry attempts exceed zero.

explanation: When both SDK tracing and API tracing are active, each request produces an anthropic.messages.create CLIENT span from the SDK and an anthropic.messages.create SERVER span from the API, both carrying token usage attributes. To prevent double-counting, token aggregation pipelines must sum spans from only one source per request (typically preferring the SERVER spans when both are available).

distractorNotes.b: Neither span performs semantic deduplication or compression; both report actual token counts from the request execution.
distractorNotes.c: Prompt caching tokens are not multiplied differently between client and server spans; the divergence is caused by summing both client and server spans.
distractorNotes.d: The SDK does not duplicate token counters on client spans across retries; final spans report total usage for the request.

sourceNote: Counting tokens: both SDK and API emit anthropic.messages.create; sum only one source to avoid double-counting

stem: A security and finance team must establish an automated accounting system to attribute monthly Claude API costs across workspaces, track usage by individual API key, and detect anomalous spending from potential key compromise. Some internal services disable OpenTelemetry trace sampling to reduce tracing vendor costs. Which mechanism provides complete, authoritative usage data for this requirement?

options.text: Stream OTLP metrics to an internal collector with trace sampling rates forced to 100 percent via collector proxy rules.
Parse client-side Anthropic SDK debug log files harvested across all production application container instances.
Query the Messages API endpoint headers for cumulative monthly token balances on each active workspace.
Query the Usage and Cost Analytics API endpoints grouped by workspace and api_key_id to capture all billed requests.

explanation: The Usage and Cost Analytics API (GET /v1/organizations/analytics/usage and /cost) provides historical, authoritative usage and cost data broken down by workspace, api_key_id, model, and actor. Unlike OpenTelemetry spans, which are delivered on a best-effort basis and subject to client-side sampling or dropping, the Analytics API captures all organizational requests (including those from clients without telemetry) with data typically fresh within 4 hours.

distractorNotes.a: A collector proxy cannot recover spans that clients dropped or failed to sample locally, and OpenTelemetry delivery is best-effort.
distractorNotes.b: Scraping client debug logs is brittle, incomplete for unmanaged scripts, and does not capture authoritative server-side billing data.
distractorNotes.c: Messages API response headers provide rate limit quotas and remaining limits, not cumulative monthly financial analytics.

sourceNote: Usage and Cost Analytics API: queries historical usage and cost by workspace and api_key_id, independent of OTel sampling

stem: A platform team deploys Claude Code across 500 developer machines exporting OpenTelemetry metrics to a central Prometheus time-series database. Within days, Prometheus experiences severe memory pressure and query degradation caused by high-cardinality label churn on session and user identifiers. Which TWO environment variables should the platform team configure in managed settings to control this cardinality explosion?

options.text: Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_VERSION to false to remove version tracking across developer CLI binaries.
Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID to false to strip session identifiers from exported metrics and events.
Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ENTRYPOINT to false to eliminate entrypoint dimensions on metric datapoints.
Set OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ACCOUNT_UUID to false to remove user account identifiers from metric time series.
Set OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL to 0 to instruct Claude Code to aggregate metrics locally before export.

explanation: In Claude Code, OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID and OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ACCOUNT_UUID both default to true, adding session.id and user.account_uuid to metrics and events. In large deployments, these attributes generate massive label cardinality in time-series databases like Prometheus. Setting them to false suppresses these high-cardinality attributes. In contrast, OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_VERSION and OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ENTRYPOINT already default to false.

distractorNotes.a: OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_VERSION defaults to false already; setting it to false does not reduce cardinality because it was not adding labels by default.
distractorNotes.c: OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ENTRYPOINT defaults to false already; it does not contribute to cardinality unless explicitly enabled.
distractorNotes.e: Setting OTEL_METRIC_EXPORT_INTERVAL to 0 does not enable local pre-aggregation; export intervals dictate flush timing in milliseconds.

sourceNote: Metrics cardinality control: OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_SESSION_ID and OTEL_METRICS_INCLUDE_ACCOUNT_UUID default to true

stem: An operations dashboard monitors Claude Code log events to detect client failures. SREs notice that alert rules trigger whenever a claude_code.api_error event is emitted. However, review reveals that some sessions continue making successful requests and complete their tasks, while other sessions stall completely. How should the team refine their event analysis to distinguish recovered sessions from stalled sessions?

options.text: Filter for api_error events where the attempt attribute is strictly greater than 15.
Check if the api_error event status_code attribute contains an HTTP 429 rate limit value.
Group events by session.id and verify whether a subsequent api_request event occurs after the api_error.
Inspect the api_retries_exhausted event to verify that the total_retry_duration_ms attribute exceeds sixty thousand milliseconds.

explanation: Claude Code retries transient API errors internally and emits an api_error event only when a particular request attempt fails terminally. However, a session may subsequently recover—for instance, if the agent or user initiates a follow-up interaction or a subsequent turn succeeds. To distinguish a session that recovered from one that halted completely, observability queries must group events by session.id and check whether any later api_request event exists after the error.

distractorNotes.a: The attempt attribute is capped at one above the effective retry limit (typically 11 by default, and maximum 16 without watchdog), so checking for values strictly above 15 is not a reliable indicator of recovery.
distractorNotes.b: The HTTP status code indicates the nature of the error (such as a rate limit), but does not reveal whether the broader session recovered or stalled on subsequent turns.
distractorNotes.d: Total retry duration reflects how long retries took on that single failed request, not whether the session resumed work afterward.

sourceNote: Detect retry exhaustion: group events by session.id and check whether a later api_request event exists after the error

stem: An enterprise routes all outbound LLM traffic through an internal AI security gateway by setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to https://ai-gateway.internal.corp/v1. The gateway is instrumented with OpenTelemetry and expects W3C trace context on inbound requests. However, spans emitted by Claude Code and spans emitted by the gateway appear as disconnected root traces in Jaeger. Which configuration enables end-to-end trace correlation?

options.text: Configure OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL to http/json so headers serialize in standard W3C text representation format.
Set CLAUDE_CODE_PROPAGATE_TRACEPARENT to 1 to force Claude Code to attach outbound traceparent headers through the custom base URL.
Add the gateway server hostname to OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES under the peer.service semantic convention attribute.
Enable OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS so model invocation parameters include the active span identifier and trace context inside JSON payload bodies.

explanation: By default, Claude Code sends the W3C traceparent header on outbound model requests and HTTP MCP requests only when ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is unset or points directly to the Anthropic API, because some custom proxies reject unrecognized headers. When routing through a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy, setting CLAUDE_CODE_PROPAGATE_TRACEPARENT=1 instructs Claude Code to propagate the traceparent header, connecting client spans to downstream proxy traces.

distractorNotes.a: OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL governs the wire protocol used to export spans to the collector, not whether outbound HTTP model calls include W3C traceparent headers.
distractorNotes.c: Setting peer.service in resource attributes labels exported spans with metadata, but does not inject W3C traceparent headers into outbound HTTP requests.
distractorNotes.d: OTEL_LOG_TOOL_DETAILS controls logging of tool input parameters in events; it does not inject W3C HTTP headers on outbound requests.

sourceNote: Trace propagation: CLAUDE_CODE_PROPAGATE_TRACEPARENT=1 propagates traceparent across custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxies

stem: A company operates complex, asynchronous multi-agent workflows using Claude Managed Agents. The application spawns multiple concurrent execution threads, and webhook callbacks from external systems trigger subsequent agent turns from distinct HTTP root requests. In an OpenTelemetry backend, an engineer must query all spans associated with a single thread, as well as all spans across the entire multi-threaded session. Which attribute pair should be used?

options.text: Use trace_id for individual conversation threads and service.name combined with deployment.environment for correlating the entire multi-threaded agent session.
Use anthropic.turn.id for individual threads and gen_ai.request.id for grouping spans across distinct HTTP root traces.
Use gen_ai.thread.id for single threads and anthropic.workspace.id for identifying all related multi-threaded operations.
Use gen_ai.conversation.id for individual threads and anthropic.session.id for correlating all threads across the entire session.

explanation: In Claude Managed Agents OpenTelemetry tracing, spans belonging to a single thread share the gen_ai.conversation.id attribute (which holds the session thread ID), allowing them to be sorted by start time as a chronological transcript. To query the entire session across all threads and across separate root traces, spans are grouped by anthropic.session.id.

distractorNotes.a: Separate turns initiated from webhook callbacks create distinct trace_id roots, so trace_id does not group a multi-turn thread, and service.name is deployment-wide rather than session-scoped.
distractorNotes.b: Neither anthropic.turn.id nor gen_ai.request.id spans multiple requests or threads; requests are grouped by conversation and session identifiers.
distractorNotes.c: The OpenTelemetry conventions and Anthropic specification use gen_ai.conversation.id (not gen_ai.thread.id) for thread correlation, and anthropic.session.id for session correlation.

sourceNote: Managed Agents spans: gen_ai.conversation.id groups one thread; anthropic.session.id groups the whole session across traces

stem: An engineering team deploys long-running coding agents that use automatic context compaction to manage conversation context windows. SREs tracking token consumption via OpenTelemetry spans notice that their token aggregation queries undercount total token consumption during compaction turns when compared directly with billing invoices. Why do standard OpenTelemetry GenAI usage attributes omit these compaction tokens?

options.text: Context compaction occurs on local client proxies and does not consume server-side model input or output tokens.
Compaction tokens are categorized as internal system infrastructure overhead and are permanently excluded from all exported OpenTelemetry spans.
The standard gen_ai.usage.* attributes exclude compaction tokens, which are reported under separate anthropic.usage.compaction.* attributes.
Compaction operations are recorded exclusively as Prometheus gauges rather than OpenTelemetry span usage attributes.

explanation: Under the Anthropic OpenTelemetry specification, standard gen_ai.usage.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.output_tokens attributes on anthropic.messages.create spans do not include tokens consumed during context compaction. Compaction token usage is reported separately under anthropic.usage.compaction.input_tokens and anthropic.usage.compaction.output_tokens (or via dedicated anthropic.compaction spans). Aggregation pipelines must sum these compaction attributes to reflect complete token consumption.

distractorNotes.a: Context compaction is performed by the model and API, consuming actual input and output tokens that are billed to the account.
distractorNotes.b: Compaction tokens are not purged; they are explicitly exported under dedicated anthropic.usage.compaction.* attributes and compaction spans.
distractorNotes.d: Compaction token metrics are exported as standard OpenTelemetry span attributes and spans, not solely as Prometheus gauges.

sourceNote: Compaction tokens: gen_ai.usage.* attributes exclude compaction tokens; add anthropic.usage.compaction.* attributes

stem: A document-summarization service calls the Messages API and reports an availability SLO of 99.5%, computed as responses without a 4xx or 5xx status over all requests. The SLO has been green for a quarter, yet support tickets about summaries that stop mid-sentence and about requests Claude declined to answer have tripled. The SRE lead wants a quality SLI whose good-event definition catches these failures without penalizing the service's multi-step tool loop, which includes server tools such as web fetch. Which definition fits?

options.text: Keep the HTTP-based availability SLI as the only SLO and chart refusals and truncations on a separate non-alerting dashboard, since both reflect user input rather than service health.
Count every response as good unless its stop_reason is refusal, max_tokens, or pause_turn, so each step of the loop is scored and truncated or stalled steps are caught.
Count a response as good when its output_tokens exceed a minimum length floor, so empty refusals and blank answers fail while substantive multi-paragraph summaries still pass.
Count a final response as good when it returns 2xx with a natural stop such as end_turn; refusal and max_tokens stops count as bad, and tool_use steps are not judged alone.

explanation: stop_reason is part of every successful Messages API response and says why generation stopped; errors are the 4xx/5xx failures. Safety classifiers return a refusal as a normal HTTP 200 response, and a max_tokens stop means the response reached the request's max_tokens limit (model_context_window_exceeded is likewise treated as truncated). A status-code SLI therefore scores both failure classes as successes. Keying the good event on the terminal stop_reason catches them, while tool_use and pause_turn are documented as signals to continue — run the tool and return the result, or send the assistant content back — so they are intermediate loop steps, not failures.

distractorNotes.a: The documentation separates stop reasons, which arrive in successful responses, from errors, which carry 4xx/5xx codes; an HTTP-only SLO is precisely what hides refusals and truncations, so keeping them off the SLO leaves the reported failures invisible to alerting.
distractorNotes.b: pause_turn means a server-tool loop reached its iteration limit and the assistant content should be sent back to continue; it is a normal continuation signal, not a stall, so counting it as bad would charge the healthy server-tool loop as failures.
distractorNotes.c: A max_tokens stop happens when the response reaches the max_tokens limit, so truncated summaries are typically long; a length floor passes exactly the mid-sentence cutoffs that users are reporting.

sourceNote: Stop reasons vs errors: refusal returns HTTP 200; max_tokens means truncation; tool_use and pause_turn are continuation signals

stem: A claims-triage service pins a current-generation dateless model ID. An online grader scores a 2% random sample of production responses against a fixed rubric and compares the daily mean with a baseline captured at launch. This week the score fell outside its control band, while the deploy log shows no prompt, tool, retrieval, or request-parameter change and API error rates are flat. An engineer argues that Anthropic must have updated the model behind the ID. Which assessment matches Anthropic's model versioning documentation?

options.text: The dateless ID is an evergreen pointer that tracks the latest snapshot of its model family, so the team should switch to a dated snapshot ID to freeze behavior.
The ID's weights are fixed, but serving infrastructure such as safety classifiers and sampling logic can change, so a shift on an unchanged ID is plausible and worth tracking.
Anthropic ships improved weights under an existing ID only after notice on the deprecations page, so checking that page will confirm whether a weight update caused the drop.
Behavior under a fixed model ID is deterministic, so a score shift with no client-side change points to grader noise, and the team should recalibrate the grader first.

explanation: Every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot: from the 4.6 generation on, the dateless ID is the canonical ID for a release and maps to a single fixed snapshot, and Anthropic does not update the weights or configuration of an existing ID — an updated version ships under a new ID. The serving infrastructure around the model (request router, safety classifiers, sampling logic) can still change, and the documentation names an infrastructure update as the most likely cause of unexpected behavioral differences on a previously stable ID. That is why a sampled grader compared against a baseline remains necessary even with a pinned ID.

distractorNotes.a: This is the misconception the documentation explicitly corrects: dateless IDs from the 4.6 generation on are not evergreen pointers but pinned snapshots, and dated IDs exist only for models before the 4.6 generation.
distractorNotes.c: Anthropic does not update the weights of an existing model ID at all; an updated version ships under a new model ID, so no weight change under the same ID exists to be announced.
distractorNotes.d: Fixed weights do not make observed behavior immutable; infrastructure components including safety classifiers and sampling logic can change and produce behavioral differences on an unchanged ID.

sourceNote: Dateless IDs are pinned snapshots; weights fixed per ID; serving infrastructure updates can shift behavior on a stable ID

stem: A legal-drafting service on the Messages API exports SDK and API spans, head-sampling 5% of traces uniformly in the application's sampler. After a configuration release, complaints about unusable drafts doubled for one enterprise tenant, yet every trace the team opens shows HTTP 200. The team wants to surface and quantify a systemic cause across the sampled population rather than by reading traces one at a time. Which TWO analyses fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Build the failure cohort from spans that carry error.type, since that attribute records each response that failed to give the user a usable answer.
Turn off the sampled flag in traceparent for healthy tenants, so the API keeps emitting their span metadata while content capture focuses on the affected tenant.
Group the tenant's anthropic.messages.create spans by anthropic.message.stop_reason and compare the share of each value with other tenants in the same sample.
Treat token sums from the sampled spans, scaled by the sampling rate, as the tenant's billed usage, since API spans carry the tokens the organization is billed for.
Segment the tenant's spans by gen_ai.response.model against gen_ai.request.model to find requests another model served, then compare outcomes by serving model.

explanation: The anthropic.messages.create span carries anthropic.message.stop_reason, so grouping a cohort by stop reason and comparing shares against other tenants in the same uniform sample exposes a shift, such as more refusal or max_tokens stops, that no single HTTP 200 trace reveals. The span also records gen_ai.response.model, which differs from gen_ai.request.model when the request uses a model alias or a fallback model served it; the API still emits one span per request in that case, so segmenting by serving model is how a routing-driven quality drop becomes visible in aggregate.

distractorNotes.a: error.type holds a failed request's error type, for example rate_limit_error; a refusal or truncation is a stop_reason on a successful response, so an error.type cohort misses exactly the HTTP 200 failures behind the complaints.
distractorNotes.b: When the sampled flag in the traceparent header is off, the API emits no span for the request or anything under it, so this removes healthy tenants from the comparison baseline instead of trimming their content.
distractorNotes.d: API spans do carry billed token counts, but exported spans are not a complete record: delivery is best effort and unsampled requests emit no API spans. Authoritative per-key usage comes from the Usage and Cost Analytics API.

sourceNote: messages.create span: stop_reason attribute; gen_ai.response.model differs on alias or fallback; error.type only on failed requests

stem: A support agent on the Messages API runs multi-turn conversations with prompt caching, under an organization-wide zero data retention arrangement. After a release, usage.cache_read_input_tokens sits near zero on most later turns. To limit what is stored, an engineer attaches the diagnostics object only to a turn whose predecessor came back with low cache reads, passing that predecessor's response id. Every diagnosed turn returns a cache_miss_reason of previous_message_not_found. All workers share one workspace, and turns are seconds apart. What does this indicate?

options.text: The predecessor turns carried no diagnostics object, so no fingerprint was stored to compare against; this is not evidence of a change, and diagnostics belongs on every turn.
The release altered the start of the prompt so deeply that no stored fingerprint matches any longer, which places the divergence in the system prompt or tool definitions.
The zero data retention arrangement blocks fingerprint storage, so lookups by previous_message_id cannot resolve and only the usage fields can be relied on for diagnosis.
The comparison was still running when each response was serialized, so every result is inconclusive and the engineer should simply read the diagnostics on the next turn.

explanation: The API stores a fingerprint only for requests that include the diagnostics object, keyed by the response id; the object itself is the opt-in. previous_message_not_found means no stored fingerprint exists for the supplied id and is explicitly not evidence that the request changed — typically the previous request lacked the diagnostics object, came from another workspace, or is too old. With one workspace and closely spaced turns, the opt-in pattern is the cause: include diagnostics on every turn, passing a null previous_message_id on the first.

distractorNotes.b: A divergence in the system prompt or tools is reported as system_changed or tools_changed against a stored fingerprint; previous_message_not_found means there was nothing to compare against.
distractorNotes.c: Cache diagnostics is ZDR eligible (qualified): fingerprints hold only cryptographic hashes and token-count estimates, never raw prompt content, so zero data retention does not prevent the comparison.
distractorNotes.d: A comparison still running at serialization time returns cache_miss_reason as null, not previous_message_not_found, so waiting for the next turn would reproduce the same result.

sourceNote: Fingerprint stored only when diagnostics is sent; previous_message_not_found is not evidence of change; ZDR eligible (qualified)
